question: How does Percival get even with O'Gallagher after he takes all of the boy's fireworks?
gold: He sets them on fire with the teacher sitting on them
final_answer:
Percival sneaks back into the empty schoolroom, lifts the claret case under which O’Gallagher has hidden the confiscated squibs and crackers, and packs additional gunpowder under it—leaving only a tiny, hard-to-notice train in the green baize.  

When O’Gallagher sits back down on the “throne,” Percival lights the train with touchwood, setting off the stored fireworks and powder so that the claret case blasts upward and O’Gallagher is “thrown up to the ceiling” in a cloud of smoke while the crackers and squibs fizz and bang (and the schoolroom catches fire).

output.summary: That evening I made known to them all that had taken place since I last wrote to them, winding up with the loss of my frigate, the death of Lord de Versely, and my subsequent capture and rescue. "And so it was in attempting to come and see us that you were wounded and nearly murdered?" question: How does Chuck end up on an island?
gold: His plane crashes and his life raft washes up on an island.
final_answer: Chuck ends up on the island because the FedEx cargo plane he’s on plummets out of the sky and crashes into the Pacific during a storm. In the wreck, his life jacket is inflated and he survives in the water as the plane sinks; afterward he’s carried by the waves and washes up on a beach (found face-down/partly buried in the sand), which is the island.

question: Why does Tellheim refuse to engage Minna von Barnhelm at first?
final_answer: Tellheim refuses at first because he believes he is no longer the “former” Tellheim Minna knew—he is now “the discharged, the suspected, the cripple, the beggar”—and therefore feels unworthy to bind her to him. He also insists he will “never…cause you to commit an imprudent [action],” i.e., he will not let Minna sacrifice herself by marrying him in his ruined, dishonoured condition.

question: How does Letitia feel about Doricourt?
gold: Letitia is hopelessly in love with Doricourt.
final_answer: Letitia is strongly drawn to Doricourt and romanticizes him—she hopes to win and “touch his heart,” not merely marry him comfortably—yet she’s also uneasy that, because he has been courted by many women, he may not feel the intense first-love passion she longs for, even though she still hopes her faithful love will move him.

gold: One where he is equally in love with her.
final_answer: Letitia is trying to draw from Doricourt a marriage founded on **Cupid’s love (a “husband of my heart”) rather than mere obligation**, i.e., to have him love her *before* and *within* marriage: “**restore the Husband of my Heart to the blessings of Liberty and Love. question: Why do the aliens refuse to study the passengers and crew of the Victory?
final_answer: The aliens refuse because they don’t want a specially selected, unrepresentative sample; they want “average/normal” humans—a cross‑section of Earth’s population (since they can’t visit Earth themselves), and a handpicked ship’s crew/passengers wouldn’t serve that purpose.

question: Why does Mrs. Hardcastle want Constance to marry her son?
gold: Keep the jewels in the family.
final_answer: Mrs. Hardcastle wants Constance to marry her son (Tony) so that Tony can “get … a part of her fortin … in jewels” (i.e., Constance Neville’s fortune, especially her jewels).

While we were eating, it came into my thoughts that while we worked at this rate in a thing of such nicety and consequence, it was ten to one if the gold, which was the make-bait of the world, did not, first or last, set us together by the ears, to break our good articles and our understanding one among another, and perhaps cause us to part companies, or worse; I therefore told them that I was indeed the youngest man in the company, but as they had always allowed me to give my opinion in things, and had sometimes been pleased to follow my advice, so I had something to propose now, which I thought would be for all our advantages, and I believed they would all like it very well. They all approved the proposal, and every one jointly swore, and gave their hands to one another, that they would not conceal the least grain of gold from the rest; and consented that if any one or more should be found to conceal any, all that he had should be taken from him and divided among the rest; and one thing more was added to it by our gunner, from considerations equally good and just, that if any one of us, by any play, bet, game, or wager, won any money or gold, or the value of any, from another, during our whole voyage, till our return quite to Portugal, he should be obliged by us all to restore it again on the penalty of being disarmed and turned out of the company, and of having no relief from us on any account whatever.

output.summary: And, to add to the exclamation I am making on the nature of the place, it was here that we took one of the rashest, and wildest, and most desperate resolutions that ever was taken by man, or any number of men, in the world; this was, to travel overland through the heart of the country, from the coast of Mozambique, on the east ocean, to the coast of Angola or Guinea, on the western or Atlantic Ocean, a continent of land of at least 1800 miles, in which journey we had excessive heats to support, unpassable deserts to go over, no carriages, camels, or beasts of any kind to carry our baggage, innumerable numbers of wild and ravenous beasts to encounter with, such as lions, leopards, tigers, lizards, and elephants; we had the equinoctial line to pass under, and, consequently, were in the very centre of the torrid zone; we had nations of savages to encounter with, barbarous and brutish to the last degree; hunger and thirst to struggle with, and, in one word, terrors enough to have daunted the stoutest hearts that ever were placed in cases of flesh and blood. We could not build anything of a vessel that would carry us over the great Arabian Sea to India, nor could we reach the Cape de Bona Speranza, the winds being too variable, and the sea in that latitude too tempestuous; but we all knew, if we could cross this continent of land, we might reach some of the great rivers that run into the Atlantic Ocean; and that, on the banks of any of those rivers, we might there build us canoes which would carry us down, if it were thousands of miles, so that we could want nothing but food, of which we were assured we might kill sufficient with our guns; and to add to the satisfaction of our deliverance, we concluded we might, every one of us, get a quantity of gold, which, if we came safe, would infinitely recompense us for our toil. My view before was, as I thought, very good, viz., that we should get into the Arabian Gulf, or the mouth of the Red Sea; and waiting for some vessel passing or repassing there, of which there is plenty, have seized upon the first we came at by force, and not only have enriched ourselves with her cargo, but have carried ourselves to what part of the world we had pleased; but when they came to talk to me of a march of 2000 or 3000 miles on foot, of wandering in deserts among lions and tigers, I confess my blood ran chill, and I used all the arguments I could to persuade them against it.

question: What is Friend William?
final_answer: “Friend William” is **William, a surgeon** whom the pirates had taken from a captured sloop and then kept with them as a “useful man,” to tend their wounds and maintain a surgeon’s chest (medical supplies), while he otherwise did not “meddle” in fighting.

output.summary: The Lady Lorna Dugal is gone, because she could not help herself; and she wept enough to break ten hearts--if hearts are ever broken, John." "Darling Lizzie, how good you are!" I cried, without noticing her sneer; "tell me all about it, dear; tell me every word she said." "That will not take long," said Lizzie, quite as unmoved by soft coaxing as by urgent cursing; "the lady spoke very little to any one, except indeed to mother, and to Gwenny Carfax; and Gwenny is gone with her, so that the benefit of that is lost. Who will thresh it out of you, and starve it, and swear it out of you!" was the meaning of my imprecation: but Lizzie, not dreaming as yet of such things, could not understand me, and was rather thankful; therefore she answered quietly,-- "The letter is in the little cupboard, near the head of Lady Lorna's bed, where she used to keep the diamond necklace, which we contrived to get stolen." Without another word I rushed (so that every board in the house shook) up to my lost Lorna's room, and tore the little wall-niche open and espied my treasure. Though they tell you I am false, though your own mind harbours it, from the sense of things around, and your own undervaluing, yet take counsel of your heart, and cast such thoughts away from you; being unworthy of itself they must be unworthy also of the one who dwells there; and that one is, and ever shall be, your own Lorna Dugal." Some people cannot understand that tears should come from pleasure; but whether from pleasure or from sorrow (mixed as they are in the twisted strings of a man's heart, or a woman's), great tears fell from my stupid eyes, even on the blots of Lorna's.

question: What role did that pollen have in nature as the insects moved from plant to plant?
gold: The pollen fertalized the different plants.
final_answer: As insects visited the mingled flower forms, the pollen stuck to their proboscides and was then deposited on the stigmas of the opposite form—thus carrying pollen from plant to plant and effecting reciprocal (cross-)fertilisation between the two forms.

In accordance with this observation I found that the two kinds of pollen, which could easily be recognised under the microscope, adhered in this manner to the proboscides of the two species of humble-bees and of the moth, which were caught visiting the flowers; but some small grains were mingled with the larger grains round the base of the proboscis, and conversely some large grains with the small grains near the extremity of the proboscis. question: How does the pollen transfer from one plant to another?
gold: The pollen attaches to the body of an insect
final_answer:
Pollen is transferred from one plant to another by a **carrier**, which the text says can be either **wind** or **insects** (“pollen can be carried… either by wind or by insects”).  

- **If wind carries the pollen**, the plants show adaptations that help pollen get blown off and caught by another plant: the pollen is **incoherent** and produced in **large quantities**, the **anthers dangle** to shake it out, the **perianth is small/absent**, the **stigmas protrude** at fertilisation, flowers are produced **before leaves** hide them, and stigmas are **downy/plumose** to catch wind-blown grains.  
- **If insects carry the pollen**, the passage contrasts this with wind-pollinated flowers and notes that insect-pollinated (especially hermaphrodite) plants have “numerous adaptations for the safe transport of the pollen by insects.”

question: What insects did Darwin observe pollinating the Cowslip?
final_answer: Darwin recorded that the cowslip (Primula veris) was pollinated by **humble-bees**—specifically **Bombus hortorum** and **Bombus muscorum**—and also by a **moth**, **Cucullia verbasci**, which was caught visiting the flowers.

output.summary: It follows from the position of the organs that if the proboscis of a dead humble-bee, or a thick bristle or rough needle, be pushed down the corolla, first of one form and then of the other, as an insect would do in visiting the two forms growing mingled together, pollen from the long-stamened form adheres round the base of the object, and is left with certainty on the stigma of the long-styled form; whilst pollen from the short stamens of the long-styled form adheres a little way above the extremity of the object, and some is generally left on the stigma of the other form. In accordance with this observation I found that the two kinds of pollen, which could easily be recognised under the microscope, adhered in this manner to the proboscides of the two species of humble-bees and of the moth, which were caught visiting the flowers; but some small grains were mingled with the larger grains round the base of the proboscis, and conversely some large grains with the small grains near the extremity of the proboscis. But to make my experiments perfectly fair, and to avoid any evil result from self-fertilisation or too close interbreeding, I have invariably employed pollen from a distinct plant of the same form for the illegitimate unions of all the species; and therefore it may be observed that I have used the term "own-form pollen" in speaking of such unions.

question: What does Shang Li do after he discovers Mulan is a woman?
gold: He sets her free because she saved his life fighting Shan Yu.
final_answer: After Shang Li realizes Mulan is a woman, he goes to her with his sword drawn—but instead of harming her, he throws the sword down in front of her and says, “A life for a life. My debt is repaid.” Then he turns away, orders the troops to “move out,” and marches on to the Imperial City, leaving Mulan behind.

question: How does Mulan prevent her father from going to the war?
final_answer: Mulan prevents her father from going to the war by secretly taking his place: she takes the conscription notice (leaving her mother’s hair comb in its place), cuts her hair short, puts on her father’s armor, and rides off to join the army herself.

question: How does Peter feel about being back in Mr. McGregor's garden?

question: How did Ellen win the final showdown with the Alien Queen?
gold: She used the exosuit ladder to expel the queen into an airlock in outer space.
final_answer: Ripley fights the Alien Queen using the Sulaco’s **power loader**, striking it with the loader’s **cutting torch**, then drags/maneuvers the Queen into a **vertical loading airlock**. She **overrides the inner door** (latching the hold/lock) and hits **“OUTER DOOR OPEN,”** causing explosive decompression that **sucks the Queen out into space**, ending the showdown.

question: Why does Augustine go to visit the Duchesse de Carigliano?
gold: To learn how the duchess captured Theodore's heart
final_answer: Augustine goes to the Duchesse de Carigliano because she is desperate about her marriage to Théodore de Sommervieux and seeks the Duchess’s help—both advice on how to “subjugate”/manage a superior, capricious artist-husband and, crucially, the return of Théodore’s portrait (which the Duchess had had and then gives back to Augustine as a “talisman” to make her “her husband’s mistress”).

question: Who is Theodore de Summervieux?
final_answer: Theodore de Sommervieux is a young, publicly recognized painter (an artist “whose name … fame had stamped on Augustine’s heart”), who becomes Augustine Guillaume’s lover (and courtship interest). He is socially elevated enough to attend fashionable balls and tries—largely unsuccessfully because of the strict Guillaume household—to gain access to Augustine and communicate with her.

question: Why are Mike and Psmith able to quit their jobs at the end of the story?
gold: Psmith's father agrees to send Psmith and Mike to school.
final_answer: They can quit because Psmith decides he has “had sufficient” of the bank and will go to Cambridge (financed by the Psmith family money), and Mike’s father plans to employ Psmith as his agent—so they have private financial backing/a new arrangement and don’t need the bank jobs.

gold: "We call him Lighnin' because he ain't"
